 Hyundai Recalls Tucson Hybrid and Elantra Vehicles for Improperly Tightened Strut Fasteners
 A fastening error at the Ulsan production complex has triggered a recall in the United States market, comprising only 24 crossovers and sedans 
 Published: 25 Oct 2026, 19:01 UTC • By: 
 Mircea Panait 
   11 photos Photo: Hyundai 
 Hyundai Motor America is recalling a handful of Elantra and Tucson Hybrid vehicles for strut assemblies that may not have been properly tightened. The automaker's campaign is referred to as 26V692 by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which lists 20 affected Elantras and four Tucson Hybrids. 
 As you're well aware, struts do a lot more than simply dampen ride motion. In vehicles with MacPherson-type front suspension, the strut connects the wheel assembly to the body, locates the steering knuckle, carries lateral loads, and absorbs impacts from road imperfections. If such fasteners are not torqued as intended, the connection ultimately loosens, leading to a catastrophic separation.
 Separating from adjoining suspension components understandably increases the risk of a crash, especially if the separation occurs at high speeds on the freeway. Affected vehicles were assembled by Hyundai in South Korea, namely at the Ulsan complex that is currently hailed as the world's largest integrated automobile manufacturing plant. Ulsan numbers six distinct manufacturing facilities.
 Production dates range from January 21 through March 20, 2026, for suspect Tucson Hybrid crossovers and December 30, 2025, through July 6, 2026, for the Elantra population. The investigation that resulted in this recall started with a field report, received by Hyundai's North American Safety Office from a 2026 model year Elantra owner.
 The customer alleged suspect noises coming from the front suspension while driving over bumps. Hyundai Motor America later surveyed potentially affected unsold vehicles through October 5, 2026, finding two vehicles with incorrectly tightened fasteners.
 Photo: Hyundai 
As for what happened at the factory, two process failures are highlighted in the recall documentation. Assembly line operator error may have left one or multiple fasteners without sufficient torque. At the same time, the torque measurement data used to confirm proper fastening was improperly recorded, preventing the system from detecting such problems.
 The involved component bears part number 62618-4D000, namely a flange nut supplied by South Korean company Samjin Nut. While the flange nut itself is not defective, insufficient torque applied during vehicle assembly makes it a ticking time bomb. Beyond a single field report, Hyundai Motor America isn't aware of any crashes or injuries related to the recall condition.
 Dealers have been instructed to check all potentially loose fasteners on both front strut assemblies. If necessary, the original parts will be retightened or replaced. The final step is to perform a wheel alignment. All of this work is free of charge, even if the vehicle is no longer under warranty. The wheel alignment, meanwhile, is necessary because strut hardware can disturb alignment settings.
 Not checking the alignment after working on the struts can lead to a pulling sensation and uneven tire wear. Hyundai says it has already changed some processes at the Ulsan complex, beginning with improved torque monitoring logic and production sign-off requirements. All of these changes were implemented on September 9, 2026.
 Customer notification letters should arrive by first-class mail no later than December 19, 2026. In the meantime, VINs of the affected crossovers and sedans are searchable on the NHTSA's recall portal.
